n: Chapters 46–51 gather Jeremiah’s prophecies against foreign nations, fulfilling his call as “a prophet unto the nations.” The God of Israel is Lord over all peoples.

f.g: The nations, non-Israelite peoples.

n: First, Egypt. This oracle concerns Pharaoh Necho’s army, defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish on the Euphrates in 605 BC—one of the turning-point battles of ancient history, which ended Egypt’s power in the region.

f.g: Necho II (about 610–595 BC), who had killed King Josiah at Megiddo.
A city on the upper Euphrates, on today’s Turkey–Syria border.

n: The poem opens with officers barking orders: prepare your shields—small and large—and advance into battle!

f.g: A small round shield; the “shield” was a larger body shield.

n: Harness the chariot horses, mount up, take your positions with helmets on, polish your spears, and put on armor!

f.g: Polish, sharpen.
Coats of armor—scale mail.

n: Suddenly the scene flips: why are they terrified and retreating? Their warriors are beaten and fleeing without looking back—terror on every side.

f.g: Hebrew magor missabib, Jeremiah’s signature phrase.
Quickly.

n: Not even the fastest or strongest can escape; they stumble and fall in the north, by the Euphrates.

f.w: Let not the swift flee away

n: Who is this rising like the Nile in flood, with surging waters?

f.g: The Nile’s annual flood was Egypt’s defining image of power.

n: It’s Egypt, boasting: “I will rise and cover the earth, destroying cities and their people.”
Charge, horses! Race, chariots! March out, warriors—Egypt’s mercenaries from Cush, Put, and Lud, skilled with shields and bows.

f.g: Hebrew Cush and Put—peoples south and west of Egypt who served as mercenaries.
Hebrew Ludim; Lydian (in western Asia Minor) or African archers.

n: But this is the Lord’s day of vengeance. The battle at the Euphrates is pictured as his “sacrifice”—a grim image of a vast slaughter that settles accounts with his enemies, including the Pharaoh who killed Josiah.

f.w: the day of the Lord GOD of hosts

f.g: Satisfied, glutted.

n: Go up to Gilead for healing balm, Egypt—but no medicine will cure you. Egypt was famous for its physicians, yet this wound is beyond them.

f.g: A healing resin from Gilead, famous in the ancient world.

n: Nations hear of Egypt’s humiliation; warriors trip over one another and fall together in panic.
A second oracle: Nebuchadnezzar will come and attack Egypt itself, not just its army abroad.

f.w: should come and smite the land of Egypt

n: Sound the alarm in Egypt’s cities—Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes: get ready, for the sword is devouring all around you. These are the very towns where Judean refugees later settled.

f.g: Memphis.

n: Why are your mighty ones swept away? They couldn’t stand, because the Lord drove them down. Some ancient versions read, “Why has Apis fled?”—Apis being Egypt’s sacred bull god.

f.g: The Greek Septuagint reads “Apis, your chosen calf,” as though Egypt’s bull-god himself had fled.

n: Soldiers stumble and fall over each other. Foreign mercenaries say, “Let’s go home to our own people, away from the oppressor’s sword.”
They mock Pharaoh: “He’s just a lot of noise—he missed his chance.”

f.w: Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise
f.g: Perhaps a pun on Pharaoh’s title: “Loudmouth who let the moment pass.”

n: The true King, the Lord of hosts, swears: as surely as Mount Tabor towers over the plain and Mount Carmel over the sea, the conqueror will come. His arrival is as certain and conspicuous as those mountains.

f.g: A prominent rounded mountain in Galilee.
A mountain ridge jutting out to the Mediterranean.

n: Pack your bags for exile, people of Egypt; Memphis will become a ruin without inhabitants.

f.g: Prepare your baggage.

n: Egypt is like a beautiful young cow, but a stinging horsefly is coming from the north. (Egypt worshipped sacred bulls, which makes the image pointed.)

f.g: Hebrew qerets—probably a gadfly or biting insect.

n: Her hired mercenaries, fat like stall-fed calves, also turn and run—their day of disaster has come.

f.g: Mercenary soldiers.

n: Egypt slithers away hissing like a snake as the enemy marches in with axes like woodcutters.

f.w: The voice thereof shall go like a serpent
f.g: Egypt’s royal crown bore a cobra (uraeus); now the snake can only hiss in retreat.

n: They will cut down her “forest”—her people and defenses—though it seems endless, because the invaders outnumber locusts.

f.g: Locusts—an image of an innumerable, devouring army.

n: Daughter Egypt will be put to shame, handed over to the people of the north.
God will punish Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh, Egypt, its gods and kings, and all who trust in Pharaoh—including Judeans who ran to Egypt for safety.

f.g: Amon of No—the chief god of No (Thebes), Egypt’s great southern religious capital.

f.w: all them that trust in him

n: Egypt will fall to Nebuchadnezzar and his officers—but afterward, God says, it will be inhabited as before. Judgment isn’t God’s final word, even for Egypt.

Then a sudden word of comfort to Israel: don’t fear, my servant Jacob. God will rescue you and your children from far-off lands; you will return and live in peace. (Repeated almost word for word from 30:10.)

f.w: fear not thou, O my servant Jacob

n: God will destroy the nations where Israel was scattered, but never completely destroy Israel. He will discipline them justly, but not abandon them.
